## The pattern: pointer map plus structured docs

The fix is structural. AGENTS.md is a brief index — what this project is, where conventions live, what to read first per task type. The knowledge itself lives in a versioned `docs/` directory.

```
AGENTS.md                    # ~100 lines: what, where, first steps
docs/
  architecture/              # ADRs, system design, key decisions
  conventions/               # Coding standards, naming, patterns
  workflows/                 # How to do common tasks
  onboarding/                # What agents need before starting a task
```

An AGENTS.md entry looks like: "For API conventions, see `docs/conventions/api.md`. For deployment procedures, see `docs/workflows/deploy.md`." The agent follows the pointer when it needs that context, rather than having it preloaded.

This follows the same principle as [retrieval-augmented context loading](../context-engineering/retrieval-augmented-agent-workflows.md): pull context when needed, not at session start.

## Enforcing freshness mechanically

Pointers only work if the linked documents exist and are current. The Harness team runs "dedicated linters and CI jobs [that] validate that the knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly," plus a recurring "doc-gardening" agent that scans for obsolete documentation and opens fix-up pull requests ([OpenAI Harness Engineering](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)). Mechanical enforcement of this kind is the same class of deterministic sensor that Martin Fowler catalogs as part of the harness: tests, linters, type checkers, and structural analysis that run fast and produce reliable signals ([Martin Fowler — Harness Engineering](https://martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html)).

Practical approaches:

- CI that breaks if AGENTS.md contains a broken link to docs/
- Lint rules that flag docs/ files not referenced from AGENTS.md
- Automated prompts to review docs/ files older than a set threshold

## When this backfires

The pointer-map pattern assumes the agent will follow pointers on demand. An ETH Zurich study of 138 Python tasks across four agents found that repository-level context files — even human-written ones — consistently raise inference cost by adding 19-20% more agent steps, and that LLM-generated context files reduced task success by ~3% on average compared to no context file at all ([Gloaguen et al. 2026, Evaluating AGENTS.md](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988v2)). The pattern is worse than the alternative when:

- The repository is small or conventional. If a single `README.md` and obvious file layout already answer "what is this and where does it live," an AGENTS.md pointer map just adds tokens without directing behavior.
- Agents do not reliably follow pointers. Some agent harnesses pre-load AGENTS.md but never traverse the linked docs, which leaves the agent with a table of contents and no content. The study found instructions are followed, but context files "do not function as effective repository overviews."
- The docs/ directory is drafted by an agent rather than maintained by humans. LLM-generated context files in the study degraded performance. Without the discipline of human authorship and the CI and doc-gardening machinery described above, the pointer map decays into stale links.

====
## Validation strategy

# Enforcing Agent Behavior with Hooks > Move critical rules out of prompts into deterministic shell hooks the model cannot override — blocking forbidden actions, rewriting inputs, and gating task completion. ## The enforcement spectrum Behavioral rules sit on a spectrum from advisory to deterministic. Most teams leave high-stakes rules at the mercy of model attention. ```mermaid graph LR A["Advisory
CLAUDE.md rules"] --> B["Probabilistic
System prompt
injection"] B --> C["Deterministic
Shell hooks
(exit code 2)"] C --> D["Organizational
Managed policies
via MDM"] style A fill:#ffeeba,stroke:#856404 style B fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style C fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#004085 style D fill:#d6d8db,stroke:#383d41 ``` Advisory — rules in CLAUDE.md or [AGENTS.md](../standards/agents-md.md). The model may ignore them under task pressure, [context compaction](../context-engineering/context-compression-strategies.md), or conflicting training priors ([Lavaee, 2025](https://alexlavaee.me/blog/openai-agent-first-codebase-learnings)). Probabilistic — system prompts or event-driven reminders. They carry higher attention weight, but still drift in long sessions ([Claude Code best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)). Deterministic — shell hooks that run outside the context window. Exit code 2 is documented to block the tool call and feed stderr back to the model ([Claude Code hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)). The model cannot argue with or forget a shell process. Coverage varies by event and tool — see [when this backfires](#when-this-backfires) for current gaps. Organizational — managed policies via MDM. They enforce organization-wide standards beyond project or user control. This is [rigor relocation](../human/rigor-relocation.md): move enforcement to a layer the model cannot influence. Every rule you shift from advisory to deterministic stops failing silently. ## Three hook patterns Claude Code hooks fire on lifecycle events (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Notification`, `Stop`) and receive JSON via stdin ([Claude Code hooks guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide)): ## Why hooks beat instructions Models revert to training defaults under pressure — attention-based architectures lose instruction compliance as the context window fills or priors conflict ([Fowler, 2025](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering.html)). I found eight issues. Three of them would stop the task working as written, so I'd fix those before you approve it. I didn't edit anything. I ran two throwaway tests in `/tmp` and deleted them afterwards.

## Fix before approving

**1. Worktree sessions have no `node_modules`, so criteria 8 and 9 can't both be met there.**
- `node_modules/` is gitignored, and the bind mount only covers the main checkout. A worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` is a fresh checkout, so `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/node_modules/rumdl/bin/rumdl` won't exist in a worktree session.
- Running `npm ci` inside the worktree would hit the same symlink-dropping mount that CLAUDE.md warns about.
- Nothing creates `node_modules` in worktrees today (there's no worktree setup hook). The existing hooks in `.claude/settings.json` call `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/node_modules/.bin/tsx`, so they probably have the same gap.
- The task should say how a worktree gets rumdl: its own install, the main checkout's copy, or an explicit fallback. It should also say what `workspaceFolder` should be there. The `workspaceFolder` setting controls which files heading search covers: in this session the harness's own rumdl server has it set to `/study/agentpatterns`, and heading search returned only files from that repo.
- Pattern: `workflows/worktree-isolation.md`. A worktree doesn't isolate the environment around it; "Every worktree still installs its own dependencies." Its "When this backfires" section lists environment setup cost.

**2. The task bundles three deliverables that are verified differently.**
- They are: the gate change (lint swap and ADR), the LSP plugin, and the `docs/tools/` doc. The gate change can be fully checked with commands. The plugin depends on an upstream Claude Code bug and on starting new sessions by hand. The doc belongs to the coach, but the board allows only one `claimed_by`.
- Under WIP=1, a blocked task still holds the slot. If the plugin work stalls, the gate change stalls with it.
- Suggested split:
  - T-0001: the lint swap and the ADR.
  - T-0002: the plugin and the Handoff results, depending on T-0001.
  - T-0003: the doc, claimed by the coach, depending on T-0002.
- Patterns:
  - `patterns/agent-design/wip-1-littles-law-agent-throughput.md`: one feature at a time, and blocked still holds the slot. Its "backfires" section covers micro-tasks and cross-cutting refactors; neither applies here.
  - `patterns/anti-patterns/pr-scope-creep-review-bottleneck.md`: one logical change per unit. Its "backfires" section notes solo teams gain less, so I rank this below finding 1.

**3. Criteria 9 and 10 can't be recorded as evidence.**
- The board requires each evidence entry to have a `command` and a `result`. "In a new Claude Code session…" names no command, and the verifier has to reproduce it.
- Fix: name the check. For example, `claude -p` asking for `documentSymbol` on a named doc, run with `--debug`, once from the main checkout and once from a worktree, with the expected output stated.
- Pattern: `instructions/feature-list-files.md`, "Validation strategy": each criterion should say which validation method applies. Its "backfires" section warns about criteria that can be met without the thing actually working.

## Worth tightening

**4. Nothing in the gate would notice if link checking stopped working.**
- Criterion 4 tests broken links with a temporary file that is then thrown away. The Context itself says rumdl is 0.x and releases every few days.
- After a future upgrade, if MD051 or MD057 stops working, `npm run check` would still pass, because a repo with 0 issues looks the same as a repo where the rule is off. The dropped `relative-links` rule is what keeps CLAUDE.md's links to docs from breaking.
- Suggestion: commit a fixture with the three broken links, excluded from `lint:md`, plus a check in the gate that expects rumdl to report all three.
- Patterns:
  - `patterns/anti-patterns/spec-complexity-displacement.md`, "What replaces verbose specs": the prose "upgrade deliberately" can't be verified; a test can.
  - `instructions/agents-md-as-table-of-contents.md`, "Enforcing freshness mechanically": CI should break on a broken link to `docs/`.

**5. Criterion 3 pins styles that oxfmt doesn't always write.**
- I ran oxfmt on a small test file, then rumdl 0.2.77 with the task's style settings. For two lists next to each other, oxfmt writes the second one with `*` to keep them separate, and rumdl then flags MD004.
- If you change that `*` to `-`, the two lists render as one list, which is the same merged-lists damage the Context blames on `rumdl fmt`.
- oxfmt also keeps `===`-underlined headings as they are. That's harmless, since it doesn't undo `#` headings either.
- Suggestion: add a criterion based on behavior, such as "Markdown written by oxfmt, including a file with two adjacent lists, passes `lint:md`". That tests the Context's stated goal ("the linter never demands a style the formatter will undo") rather than four values chosen in advance.
- Pattern: `spec-complexity-displacement.md` again. Use a check that verifies, not prose that describes.

**6. rumdl's own output tells agents to run the formatter the task keeps out of the workflow.**
- On a failure, `rumdl check` ends with "Run `rumdl fmt` to automatically fix all 2 issues."
- Criterion 6 only keeps `rumdl fmt` out of scripts, hooks and CI. It does nothing about an agent that reads the gate's failure and follows that hint.
- I wouldn't add a hook yet, because nobody has seen it happen. I'd do two things now:
  - Have the implementer check whether rumdl can turn that hint off.
  - Have the `docs/tools/` doc say "don't run `rumdl fmt`; use `npm run format`."
- If agents run it anyway, a Bash hook that blocks `rumdl fmt` and `rumdl check --fix` is the next step.
- Pattern: `instructions/enforcing-agent-behavior-with-hooks.md`. Rules that are simple yes/no belong in hooks. Its "backfires" section warns about false positives and hooks that fail open.

**7. The new doc has no path from CLAUDE.md, and its "not working" markers will go stale.**
- The acceptance criteria only add `tools/` to `docs/README.md`. But CLAUDE.md doesn't link to `docs/README.md`; it only links to `docs/decisions/`. So an agent is unlikely ever to find the LSP guide.
- Suggestion: add a criterion for one pointer line in CLAUDE.md under "Where things are". I'd write that line, since I maintain CLAUDE.md.
- "Marks any operation … not working, with the Claude Code version" will be wrong after the next Claude Code update. Keep the version-specific status in the task's Handoff and keep the doc to lasting facts, such as asking for backlinks from a body line rather than a heading. Where the doc repeats plugin settings, it must be updated whenever those settings change.
- Patterns:
  - `instructions/agents-md-as-table-of-contents.md`. Its "backfires" section notes agents don't reliably follow pointers, so the pointer has to be at the top level.
  - `patterns/anti-patterns/stale-ai-configuration-artifacts.md`.
  - `instructions/plugin-component-co-change.md`: where prose restates how the implementation behaves, it must change with it, or the detail should be stripped.
  - `context-engineering/discoverable-vs-nondiscoverable-context.md`: don't restate what `.lsp.json` already shows.

## Minor

**8. Some research in the Context is second-hand.**
- The plugin layout, and whether `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` works inside `.lsp.json` `args`, come from a research subagent and are marked "verify while implementing." The plugin examples I've seen use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, so this is the claim most likely to be wrong.
- Suggestion: say what the implementer does if it fails, and whether that means moving the task to `blocked/` or choosing another way to start the server.
- Otherwise the Context is well aimed. It records facts an agent can't get from the repo: the upstream bug, the formatter conflict, and the symlink-dropping mount.
- Pattern: `patterns/anti-patterns/assumption-propagation.md`, the "spec itself is wrong" case under "When this backfires". Its mitigation ladder notes that spec-first work only catches misreadings, not wrong requirements.

**Checked and fine:**
- The new ADR plus a link from ADR 0001 follows 0001's own "Changing any of these tools needs a new ADR."
- The exact version pin fits ADR 0001.
- Adding the plugin to `.claude/settings.json` needs your OK, and approving the task counts as that.
